extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners referencing examiner guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claim additional elements amount to 'significantly more' than a judicial exception under the Alice/Mayo Step 2B framework. Focused on identifying well-understood, routine, conventional activity, meaningful limitations, and mere instructions to apply an exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether additional elements in a claim amount to significantly more than a judicial exception, evaluate whether the elements define only well-understood, routine, conventional activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consideration overlaps with improvement, mere-instructions-to-apply, and insignificant-extra-solution-activity considerations (see MPEP §§2106.05(a), (f), (g)). Key points: (1) An additional element known in the art can still be unconventional or non-routine — novelty/obviousness are separate inquiries. (2) A prior art search should not ordinarily be necessary; examiners may rely on what courts or those skilled in the art recognize as well-understood, routine, conventional activity. An examiner should only conclude an element is well-understood/routine/conventional when they can readily conclude, based on their expertise, that the element is widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant industry. (3) Even if individual elements are conventional, their combination may be an inventive concept (new combination may be patentable). The specification may indicate elements are conventional; courts sometimes treat conventionality as appropriate for judicial notice. Examiners should explain Step 2B conclusions when appropriate and see MPEP §2106.07(a) for formulating rejections involving this consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receiving or transmitting data over a network
rubrics_metrics.description: Receiving or transmitting data over a network (e.g., using the Internet to gather data) has been recognized by courts as a well-understood, routine, conventional computer function when claimed in a generic manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples: Symantec (utilizing intermediary computer to forward information), TLI Communications (telephone for image transmission), OIP Techs. (sending messages over a network), buySAFE (computer receives and sends information over a network). Caveat: DDR Holdings distinguished claims that specify how Internet interactions are manipulated to yield a desired result (i.e., specifics may avoid being labeled generic). Analyze with other Step 2B considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performing repetitive calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a computer to perform repetitive calculations can be a conventional computer function when recited at a generic level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: Flook (recomputing/readjusting alarm limit values), Bancorp Services v. Sun Life (computer used only for basic repetitive calculations does not impose meaningful limits). If the claimed computation imposes meaningful limits or specific improvements, it may not be merely conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic recordkeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronic recordkeeping (e.g., creating and maintaining shadow accounts or updating an activity log) is recognized as well-understood, routine, conventional activity when claimed generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: Alice (creating/maintaining 'shadow accounts'), Ultramercial (updating an activity log). Consider whether the claim adds non-generic, meaningful limitations beyond mere recordkeeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storing and retrieving information in memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Storing and retrieving information in memory, when recited generically, has been recognized as a conventional computer function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: Versata Dev. Group v. SAP, OIP Techs. Examiners should assess whether storage/retrieval is recited at a high level of generality or is part of a non-generic combination that provides technical improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronically scanning or extracting data from a physical document
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronically scanning or extracting data from a physical document (e.g., OCR) is a recognized conventional activity when claimed at a high level of generality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Content Extraction and Transmission v. Wells Fargo (optical character recognition). Evaluate whether the claim recites specific technical improvements in how scanning/extraction is performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Web browser back and forward button functionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Browser back/forward button functionality is an example of a well-understood, routine, conventional computer function when claimed generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Internet Patent Corp. v. Active Network. Consider whether the claim adds a non-generic manner of implementing such functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining the level of a biomarker in blood by any means
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining a biomarker level in blood (by any means) is a life-sciences laboratory technique courts have recognized as well-understood, routine, conventional when claimed generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: Mayo (determination of metabolites), Cleveland Clinic Foundation v. True Health Diagnostics. If the claim ties the measurement to a specific, unconventional application or integrates it into a meaningful limitation, it may be significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to amplify and detect DNA
rubrics_metrics.description: PCR amplification and detection of DNA is recognized as a conventional laboratory technique when recited generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Genetic Techs. v. Merial; Ariosa v. Sequenom. Examiners should determine whether there is a non-generic application or unconventional technique that makes the claim significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting DNA or enzymes in a sample
rubrics_metrics.description: Detecting DNA or enzymes in a sample is a well-understood laboratory activity when claimed at a high level of generality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities: Sequenom; Cleveland Clinic Foundation. Assess whether the claim adds meaningful limitations beyond the generic detection step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immunizing a patient against a disease
rubrics_metrics.description: Immunizing a patient is a conventional life-sciences activity recognized by courts when claimed generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Classen Immunotherapies v. Biogen IDEC. Consider if the immunization step integrates analysis into a specific and tangible application (which may be meaningful).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyzing DNA to provide sequence information or detect allelic variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyzing DNA to obtain sequence information or detect allelic variants is a recognized conventional laboratory activity when recited generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: Genetic Techs. Evaluate whether claimed analysis is performed in a novel, unconventional manner or integrated into a meaningful application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freezing and thawing cells
rubrics_metrics.description: Freezing and thawing cells (including repeated freeze/thaw steps) is a lab technique courts have treated as conventional when claimed generically, though particular non-routine combinations may be inventive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Rapid Litigation Management v. CellzDirect (repeating steps contrary to prior art was not routine). Examine whether the claimed repetition or arrangement departs from conventional practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amplifying and sequencing nucleic acid sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Amplifying and sequencing nucleic acids is a well-understood technique when claimed in a generic manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Univ. of Utah Research Foundation v. Ambry Genetics. Assess for specific, unconventional methods or improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybridizing a gene probe
rubrics_metrics.description: Hybridizing a gene probe is a routine laboratory activity when recited generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Ambry Genetics. Determine whether the claim recites a non-generic application or improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording a customer’s order
rubrics_metrics.description: Recording a customer's order is an example of other activity courts have found to be well-understood, routine, conventional when claimed generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Apple v. Ameranth. Consider whether the claimed way of recording provides a specific technological improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shuffling and dealing a standard deck of cards
rubrics_metrics.description: Shuffling and dealing a standard deck of cards is a conventional activity when claimed generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: In re Smith. Claims that merely recite such conventional activities without more are likely not to add significantly more than an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restricting public access to media by requiring a consumer to view an advertisement
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring a consumer to view an advertisement to access media has been treated as routine activity when claimed generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Ultramercial v. Hulu. Evaluate whether the claimed mechanism adds meaningful limitation or is mere routine activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying undeliverable mail items, decoding data, and creating output data
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifying undeliverable mail items, decoding data on those items, and creating output data is an example of activity courts have found routine when recited generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Return Mail, Inc. v. U.S. Postal Service. Examine whether the claim recites specific, unconventional processing that would be significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presenting offers and gathering statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting offers and gathering statistics has been recognized as conventional activity when claimed at a high level of generality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: OIP Techs. Consider whether the claim ties these activities to a particular inventive manner of implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining an estimated outcome and setting a price
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining an estimated outcome and setting a price is an example of routine activity when claimed generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: OIP Techs. Analyze whether a claimed specific method of estimation/price-setting provides a meaningful limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arranging a hierarchy of groups, sorting information, eliminating less restrictive pricing information and determining the price
rubrics_metrics.description: Arranging hierarchies, sorting information, eliminating less restrictive pricing info, and determining price are activities courts have recognized as conventional when recited generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Versata Dev. Group v. SAP. Determine whether the claimed combination or arrangement provides a non-conventional technical improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other meaningful limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: For a claim directed to a judicial exception to be patent-eligible, it must include additional features that add meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the exception to a technological environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meaningful limitations are those that provide an inventive concept and transform the judicial exception into a practical application (examples: Diehr — Arrhenius equation integrated into automated rubber-molding steps; Classen — immunization step that integrated analysis into a tangible method). In contrast, claims that only link to a computer or other generic environment (Alice) or recite conventional data-gathering (OIP) do not meaningfully limit. Examiners must consider additional elements both individually and in combination; a combination may amount to significantly more even if individual elements do not. When appropriate, examiners should explain on the record why additional elements meaningfully limit the judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere instructions to apply an exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether additional elements amount to more than reciting the words 'apply it' (or equivalent)—i.e., whether they are more than mere instructions to implement an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon (for example, implementation on a generic computer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court precedent (Mayo, Alice, Benson) holds that simply adding instructions to apply an exception (e.g., measure metabolite levels by any means; implement intermediated settlement on a generic computer) does not make the claim eligible. Examiners should guard against §101 analyses that turn on drafting art. Requiring more than mere instructions does not demand narrow claims; some broad claims have been held eligible when they recite technical improvements (e.g., McRO, Thales Visionix). This consideration often overlaps with improvement, particular machine/transformation, and well-understood routine conventional considerations; evaluate all relevant Step 2B factors. If limitations do not amount to more than 'apply it', explain why they do not meaningfully limit the claim in the rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that recites only the idea of a solution or outcome—failing to recite details of how the solution is accomplished—is equivalent to merely saying 'apply it' and does not provide significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: Electric Power Group (caution against result-focused claims that effectively cover any solution), Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec, Internet Patents Corp. v. Active Network. By contrast, claiming a particular solution or way to achieve the outcome may provide significantly more. Example: Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One (claims describing modifications to underlying XML documents lacked specific steps and were held ineligible). Examiners should look for lack of mechanism, overly result-oriented language, or absence of specific steps as indications the claim merely recites an outcome.
